The newspaper's all-encompassing wording should **not** be treated as a precise description of which defendants were exonerated.  
**Assessment:** **Well-established broader historical affair**, with a specific contemporaneous American newspaper report of the reversal. Further legal-judgment comparison would be valuable.

**Source:** *New-Hampshire Gazette*, p. 2 â€” [original page](https://www.loc.gov/resource/sn83025587/1787-07-07/ed-1/?sp=2).  
**Report:** A London account dated April 20 described a Dr. Meggs abruptly returning from the Isle of Wight after imagining that his wife and child had been murdered. **Source:** *The National Intelligencer and Washington Advertiser*, p. 3 â€” [original page](https://www.loc.gov/resource/sn83045242/1804-01-13/ed-1/?sp=3).  
**Report:** A proclamation dated **November 29, 1803**, bearing the names **Dessalines, Christophe, and Clervaux**, acknowledged that some inhabitants had been killed amid the upheavals in Saint-Domingue. It expressed regret and maintained that the violence was contrary to the leaders' wishes and difficult to prevent during war.  
**Assessment:** **Primary-period publication of leaders' political defense**, not independent proof of their command responsibility or lack of it. **Follow-up open.**

seed_heading: A correspondent describes a short, violent Jamaica earthquake
audit_status: No conflict in saved summary located; article comparison remains OPEN
discovery_title: January 1, 1805 â€” A correspondent describes a short, violent Jamaica earthquake
discovery_body:
**Source:** *The New Hampshire Gazette*, p. 4 â€” [original page](https://www.loc.gov/resource/sn83025588/1805-01-01/ed-1/?sp=4).  
**Report:** A letter reprinted from the *Kingston (Jamaica) Royal Gazette* described a single strong tremor lasting about four seconds, unusual atmospheric stillness, and agitated animals. It placed the shock at **11:05 p.m. on a Thursday the 30th**, but the original letter's publication month is not evident from the reprint.  
**Assessment:** **Dated American reprint of a first-person natural-phenomenon report**; the original Jamaican issue, date, and independent seismic record are not checked. **Follow-up open.**

audit_status: No conflict in saved summary located; article comparison remains OPEN
discovery_title: July 24, 1806 â€” A bogus banknote is used to purchase a horse
discovery_body:
**Source:** *The Statesman* (London), p. 4, British Library digitized OCR â€” [source collection and downloadable year file](https://bl.iro.bl.uk/entities/product/2252a010-5953-4c65-8993-1be3da97d935).  
**Report:** A court dispatch described a seller accepting a purported banknote as payment for a horse, only to discover it was a fake instrument styled as a **â€œDebtors' Bankâ€** note. The newspaper reported a conviction. The accused contended that he could not read and had been deceived by whoever gave him the note.  
**Assessment:** **Newspaper report of a particular court result**; the defendant's identity is difficult to read in OCR, and original court papers have not been consulted. **Follow-up open.**

discovery_title: July 24, 1806 â€” Newspaper accuses rivals of manipulating peace rumors and public funds
discovery_body:

Stocking** being hanged in connection with the murders of **Cephas Farenbaugh** and **John Rose**. **Assessment:** **Substantive published follow-up to HN-170 and HN-173.** The earlier accounts render **Driskill** as **Driscoll**, a spelling discrepancy still to reconcile. The report supersedes the earlier uncertainty over whether their death sentences were carried out, but does **not** by itself validate the trial evidence or fix the precise execution date. **Underlying case files remain unreviewed.**

**Assessment:** The **Dutchman's Curve** wreck happened. Tennessee's commemorative record cites **101 dead**, a count it also notes has been challenged over time. **Source:** *Indianapolis News*, p. 27 â€” [original page](https://newspapers.library.in.gov/?a=d&d=INN19181004-01.1.27); [CDC pandemic history](https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/flu/pandemic-resources/1918-commemoration/1918-pandemic-history.htm).  
**Report:** Under a headline about closing public places, the paper described **crowded hospitals, shortages of medical staff, and thousands of workers absent** at the Hog Island shipyard as influenza spread. Restricting gatherings was becoming an emergency public-health tool.  
**Assessment:** This is an authentic report of the **1918 influenza pandemic**, later estimated by CDC to have caused roughly **675,000 U.S. deaths and at least 50 million worldwide**. The specific shipyard absence figure is a **contemporary operational report**, not a verified census of infections. There was no influenza vaccine then.

**Report:** A dispatch on violent attacks and retaliation in Chicago said **27 people had died**, described serious injuries, troops standing by, and disturbances in Black and other neighborhoods. Its headline portrayed the entire city as descending into disorder.  
**Assessment:** The **1919 Chicago race riot** followed the death of **Eugene Williams**, a Black teenager attacked at a segregated Lake Michigan swimming area. The later accepted total is **38 dead**, with **23 Black and 15 white victims**. Much of the violence targeted Black Chicagoans; the first report's 27 was provisional.

**Report:** A front-page headline announced that the **Tennessee legislature had ratified women's suffrage**, completing the required three-fourths of state approvals.  
**Assessment:** **August 18** was the decisive ratification date; the federal proclamation followed on **August 26** (HN-422). **Assessment:** The National Archives records certification on **August 26, 1920**; the item was **printed August 27**. The headline's sweeping language did not mean that all American women could actually cast ballots without discrimination, nor does the 27-million estimate establish newly enfranchised voters.

**Report:** A dispatch from **Tulsa, Oklahoma**, announced martial law and a grand-jury investigation after an alleged **nearly 100 deaths** and massive property damage. The newspaper used the contemporary **'race riot'** terminology, describing authorities attempting to assign blame.  
**Assessment:** This was the **Tulsa Race Massacre**: white attackers destroyed much of **Greenwood**, an affluent Black district, and killed Black residents. Casualty estimates remain contested and no first-day figure is definitive. The NPS recounts both the early low official count and later higher estimates, and the underlying attack must not be presented as two equally situated mobs.

Another, citing reports from the nearby town of Sumner, said a mob had **burned almost the entire village**. Both accounts were composed while violence and flight continued.  
**Assessment:** The Florida State Archives documents a **racially motivated white-mob massacre and destruction of Rosewood's Black community**. The **22 figure was an early, unverified estimate**, not a verified victim list. Labeling the event a generic, symmetrical 'race riot' conceals who was targeted; later survivor accounts are essential.

seed_heading: Japan earthquake dispatch claims 250,000 deaths
audit_status: No conflict in saved summary located; article comparison remains OPEN

discovery_body:
